summary:
Lima stands under the national framework of Peru. Trans identity is not criminalised there, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising. A trans visitor to the capital is answerable to rules set by Peru's Congress and enforced by national and municipal authorities rather than by the Municipalidad Metropolitana de Lima itself.

In February 2025 the Congress Women and Family Commission approved unanimously, for plenary debate, the dictamen of bills on bathroom access presented by Jorge Montoya of Honor y Democracia, which bars trans people from facilities not matching their biological sex at birth. The text also obliges removal of "ambiguous" signage of the kind Lima's Jorge Chávez international airport had placed, wording such as "for all persons with female identity" or "male identity". The April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents then mandated that restroom entry be determined by biological sex, barring trans people, including trans youth, from facilities matching their gender identity, and the same legislative package bans inclusive signage such as "women in their diversity".

Activist Gianna Camacho warns that enforcement will amount to identity-document (DNI) checks by security staff deciding who may enter a bathroom, a judgement she calls discriminatory and based on prejudice. The restriction reaches private life as well: a consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy, and on television presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to "go use the men's room".

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. The Observatory recorded 54 murders of LGBTI people and 170 reported rights violations in Peru between 2020 and 2023, with trans women the most affected: 30 of the 54 killed. Nineteen homicides were recorded in 2023, and no suspects were identified in 26 of the killings. The state keeps no system recording the sexual orientation of people killed. In the capital the pattern is visible: on 12 February 2023 the "Los Gallegos" gang kidnapped the trans sex worker Rubí Torres Silvano, 31, from jirón Chancay in central Lima and killed her with roughly 30 gunshots.

Justice machinery has produced one landmark outcome. In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history; the case reached the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

Speech and association are constrained. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years. Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.
tangentialFactors:
Regional standards run against the domestic statute. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights. The human-rights institute IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru found that the bathroom provision openly discriminates against trans and non-binary people by barring access to facilities matching their gender identity, implicitly framing them as harassment risks, and recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu.

The 2017 repeal of LGBT coverage from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions was carried by Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. The outcome left Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

Data caveats travel with the violence figures. Co-author of the 2024 report Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender, stressed that recorded figures are only a sub-registry, and the absence of any state system recording the sexual orientation of killing victims means totals are minimums rather than counts.
localsOnly:
Residents live with the 2017 removal of LGBT protections from the Penal Code's hate-crime provisions and with the April 2025 law's censorship provisions, whose vague child-protection articles and article 4 ban on media and advertising content apply to domestic publishing, advertising and artistic production; the minimum sentence for obscenity rose from three to four years.

Domestic redress routes are narrow in practice. A consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym enforcing the bathroom policy, and the state maintains no system recording the sexual orientation of people killed, so resident-side violence data depend on civil-society observatories.

Healthcare guidance improved in June 2024 when Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official guidance, a change framed as a step toward dignity for trans patients. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, acting on an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved in these sources: whether the April 2025 bathroom provision has been challenged before Peru's Constitutional Tribunal, and whether the July 2025 ruling against an anti-equality decree bears on it.

Unresolved: whether the obligation to remove "ambiguous" signage binds facilities of the Municipalidad Metropolitana de Lima itself, or only private and national operators. The sources describe signage at the Jorge Chávez international airport without stating who must comply.

Not sourced: any documented instance in Lima of security staff demanding a DNI at a bathroom entrance. The claim is Gianna Camacho's warning about how enforcement will operate, not a recorded case.

Not sourced: whether the dismissed gym complaint was appealed or whether the dismissal is final.

Unresolved: violence totals stop at 2023 in the available inventory, and no sourced count for 2024 or 2025 exists here; with no state recording system for orientation of victims, any figure is a floor.
